source.title: Scaling Laws with Vocabulary: Larger Models Deserve Larger Vocabularies
source.authors: Chao-Fan Tao; Qian Liu; Long-Xu Dou; Niklas Muennighoff; Zhong-Wei Wan; Ping Luo; Min Lin; Ngai Wong

page_placements.theme: Tokenization, resolution and input allocation change effective scale

record.tranche_reason: The study measures vocabulary-aware language-model loss and compute-optimal allocations using a modified loss metric and a setup that adds vocabulary size to the scaling analysis.
record.gate_note: The paper also cites scaling-law results from other work; those cited findings are not recorded as rows. The allocation curves and some loss results are presented in figures without individually stated numerical values. The downstream comparisons in Tables 2 and 3 report task-level results as well as averages; the rows below record the reported averages.
record.test_reason: The study fits IsoFLOPs power laws for compute-optimal allocation across 33M–1.13B non-vocabulary-parameter models, which bears on V3. It also relates normalized pretraining loss and compute to downstream accuracy, which bears on V6. Its method differs from the originals: vocabulary parameters are split out, loss is unigram-normalized, and data is counted in characters.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also predict that most public LLMs use too small a vocabulary; for example, Llama2-70B should have at least 216K rather than 32K. They validate their predictions only up to about 3B parameters.
record.recipe_differences: The study extends scaling analysis to vocabulary parameters, uses unigram-normalized loss and training characters, and fits three allocation or loss-prediction approaches rather than reproducing either original study's setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The empirically preferred vocabulary size changes with training-data availability: the Nnv = 302M example shifts from 16K to 10K when data is limiting and from 16K to 24K with excessive data. The paper also uses three different approaches to predict vocabulary allocation.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed FLOPs, loss has an interior optimum in vocabulary size, and that optimum shifts upward with budget.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The compute-optimal vocabulary size grows with compute.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimal vocabulary parameters scale as C^0.42, slower than non-vocabulary parameters (γ≈0.83–0.84).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Vocabulary parameters should scale sublinearly in non-vocabulary parameters.

fits_no_version.finding: At Nnv=302M the best vocabulary moves from 16K to 10K with scarce data and from 16K to 24K with excess data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The optimal vocabulary depends on the amount of training data.

fits_no_version.finding: Predicted vocabulary sizes beat 32K on average downstream accuracy at three budgets (48.5 vs 47.9, 43.9 vs 43.2, 51.6 vs 50.3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Vocabulary allocation improves downstream accuracy at fixed compute.

record.problems: The authors state that the pretraining experiments have no error bars because repeating runs across model sizes, vocabulary sizes, training-character counts, and repetitions would be prohibitively expensive. The scaling fits use a limited experimental range and include interpolated configurations. The paper notes limits in the granularity and range of available data points and reports that its larger-model empirical validation reaches 3B parameters.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports additional task-level accuracies and standard deviations in Tables 2 and 3; the rows record the reported average rather than creating separate rows for every task. Figure 7 also plots loss values across vocabulary sizes and budgets without textually specified values for each point; the explicitly described vocabulary shifts are recorded in R5 and R6.

untested.parts: The power-law loss form is assumed (a modified Chinchilla formula with α1=β), not tested. No fit quality or loss-vs-scale curves are reported for standard cross-entropy or for Lu.
No loss predicted from small runs is compared against the observed loss of larger runs. The 2.87B validation reports only downstream accuracy.
Equal scaling of parameters and data is imposed by constraint, so Kaplan vs Hoffmann is not adjudicated. Data is measured in characters, and the range is only 33M–1.13B Nnv.
Depth/width insensitivity is assumed from Kaplan to fix the embedding dimension; it is not tested.
Only English text pretraining is used; no other modalities or training regimes.
There is no comparison of how fitting choices change exponents or the compute-optimal split, and no test for curvature away from a power law.

missing.what: Standard LM loss correlates positively with downstream accuracy across vocabulary sizes, i.e. the reverse of the expected direction.
Approach 2 power law of optimal Nv vs Nnv, with γ=0.83, and its agreement with Approaches 1 and 3.

record.verdict_notes: The study adopts Kaplan/Chinchilla power-law forms as assumptions and extends them to vocabulary. Its V3 evidence is the power-law form of the optimal allocation; the equal-scaling split is a constraint it imposed, not a finding. V1 is treated as assumed rather than tested because no fit quality is reported for Approach 3.

versions.untested_parts: The study fits a vocabulary-aware, unigram-normalized loss formula; it does not test ordinary cross-entropy independently against parameters, tokens, and compute with the other variables held non-limiting.
It does not test whether power laws fitted on small runs predict the held-out loss of runs orders of magnitude larger.

The allocation fit uses training characters rather than directly fitting token counts, and its fitted model-size range is limited to non-vocabulary parameter counts from 33M to 1.13B. It does not compare Kaplan and Hoffmann laws across their original setups.
Architecture details such as depth and width are not varied to test their effect on loss.
The study uses English text pretraining; it does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer as settings for the same power-law form.
The study reports a relationship between normalized pretraining loss and downstream performance, but does not test whether downstream performance scales predictably with model scale.
It does not test whether published scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits disagree because of fitting choices, nor whether curves bend away from a single power law.

rows.subject: Approach 3 vocabulary-dependent loss fit (models with Nnv from 33M to 1.13B)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a vocabulary-aware parametric formula to unigram-normalized validation loss using non-vocabulary parameters, vocabulary parameters, and training characters.
rows.measure: Fitted unigram-normalized loss: Lu = −E + A1/Nnv^α1 + A2/Nv^α2 + B/D^β, with D = Hf(V)
rows.note: The fitted loss formula contains inverse-power terms for non-vocabulary parameters, vocabulary parameters, and training data. It is a joint, vocabulary-aware fit rather than a separate test of ordinary cross-entropy scaling with each variable.
rows.check: The Chinchilla-style form is adopted, with α1=β imposed, and only coefficients are reported. No goodness of fit or loss-vs-scale curve is given for Approach 3, so the row cannot show loss following a power law.

rows.subject: Approach 1 compute-optimal allocation fit (models with Nnv from 33M to 1.13B)
rows.operation_detail: Fit power laws to selected minimum-loss allocations across IsoFLOPs budgets.
rows.measure: Compute-optimal non-vocabulary parameters, vocabulary parameters, and training characters as functions of FLOPs C
rows.note: The paper reports these fitted relationships and says non-vocabulary parameters and training characters scale equally, while vocabulary parameters scale more slowly.
rows.check: The power-law form of the optimal allocations is fitted with reported low RMSE and high R². However, the equal Nnv/H exponent (0.50/0.50) is imposed ('we set α1 = α3'), not measured. Fits also use interpolated points and count data in characters.

rows.subject: Models with fixed Nnv and embedding dimension, varying vocabulary sizes
rows.size_stated: Fixed Nnv within each model family; families listed in Table 4
rows.operation_detail: Compare downstream-task performance with final language-model loss and unigram-normalized loss.

conditions.value: 7 downstream tasks: WG, PIQA, OBQA, Hellaswag, BoolQ, ARC-E, ARC-C

rows.measure: Relationship between downstream performance and unigram-normalized pretraining loss
rows.value: The paper reports that lower Lu is associated with better downstream performance across the plotted tasks; numerical correlations are not stated in the text.
rows.uncertainty: Confidence intervals are shown in Figure 13; numerical interval values are not stated in the text.
rows.note: The text explicitly describes the expected negative relationship for Lu, but gives no task-specific numerical correlation values.
rows.check: Figure-only result: a regression of downstream accuracy on Lu across vocabulary sizes at fixed Nnv. No numerical correlation is given.

rows.subject: Models with fixed Nnv and varying vocabulary sizes
rows.operation_detail: Interpolate observed loss points to compare vocabulary sizes at fixed FLOPs budgets.
rows.measure: Loss as vocabulary size changes at a fixed FLOPs budget; location of the minimum
rows.value: The loss first falls and then rises with vocabulary size; the vocabulary at the minimum increases as the FLOPs budget increases.
rows.note: The text describes an interior vocabulary optimum that shifts upward with compute, but does not provide numeric loss values.

relationships.condition: IsoFLOPs fits, Nnv 33M–1.13B, SlimPajama, unigram-normalized loss, data in characters
relationships.reason: R2: optimal Nnv, Nv and H each fit power laws in C with low RMSE and high R². The equal Nnv/H exponent is imposed, not found.
relationships.display_finding: Optimal vocabulary parameters, non-vocabulary parameters, and training characters fit compute power laws with low error and high R², while equal non-vocabulary and character exponents were imposed.

relationships.reason: R3: lower Lu goes with better downstream accuracy. R9/R7/R11: average accuracy rises 43.2→47.9→50.3 as compute grows.
relationships.display_finding: Lower loss accompanies better downstream accuracy, and average accuracy rises from 43.2 to 47.9 to 50.3 as compute increases.
